text: hey everybody one of the most common things I'm asked is what Bible translations I would recommend and there are a few different options that I tend
to recommend if you're just looking for a Hebrew Bible I think right now Robert alter's translation of the Hebrew Bible is one of the best out there and it has
a lot of great explanatory uh contextualizing notes although they tend to be a lot more literally oriented
another good choice is the Jewish publication Society or JPS Tanakh now that's available in a Jewish Study Bible
that also has a lot of good book introductions and explanatory notes and things like that but be aware that the JPS Tanakh gives priority to the
traditional masoretic text so they're going to be a lot of places where it preserves a more traditional reading where Scholars are in pretty
widespread agreement that something like the Septuagint or the Dead Sea Scrolls preserves a more original reading and so
alter is going to side with that scholarship a lot more frequently so the those are two Hebrew Bibles that I would
recommend if you're looking for a Hebrew Bible and a new testament together I think the best translation available right now is the new revised Standard
Version and the best addition I would say is the New Oxford annotated Bible and specifically the most recent fifth edition which has a number of good book
introductions and explanatory notes as well as thematic essays in the back now the new revised Standard Version just came out with an updated Edition
that makes a handful of small adjustments here and there and that has yet to be incorporated into the Oxford
annotated Bible series so I imagine there will be a sixth edition coming out in the next few years that incorporates the updated Edition so some people may
want to wait on that if you're looking for a new testament uh I think the nrsv's New Testament is decent there's
not really any outstanding new translation of the New Testament that has come out recently David Bentley Hart recently published a translation of the New Testament
that seeks to try to recreate the experience of the original Greek reader so if the Greek is very polished and
sophisticated then the English translation is going to be polished and sophisticated whereas if it is really stilted and awkward as in the Book of
Revelation the English translation is going to be stilted and awkward so it's not the most accessible translation in the world but for what it's trying to do
I think it does a good job if you just want the gospels there is an interesting translation by Sarah Rudin who is a phenomenal translator called the gospels
and this translation I think is a lot more accessible it's more idiomatic however it does do things like use
transliterations of names and place names so it's not the traditional names you're used to seeing and it includes diacritics and things like that in
transliteration so you might try that out if you're not interested in the nrsv the new English translation is also an interesting translation I have concerns
with the translation and many places however it is filled with copious footnotes explaining translation choices
explaining the backgrounds of different debates about how to translate and how to understand certain words and
Concepts and so if you're interested in finding out what the arguments are what the disagreements are the new English translation is probably going to be the
best way to find that out without investing in a full commentary now in addition to a good study Bible I would
also recommend an introduction to these texts a good introduction to the Hebrew Bible is one by John Collins which is in
a third edition that's pretty accessible I also really like David Carrs an introduction to the Old Testament which
discusses it from the perspective of literature and Empire and things like that so it's really interesting on the New Testament I think Bart ehrman's a
brief introduction to the New Testament is very good another thing that I would recommend for folks who want to understand the context of the creation
of the Bible in its interpretation is John Barton's book a history of the Bible which does a phenomenal job of
talking about the background of the text how they were developed how they came together how the Canon developed and then how they have been interpreted
historically within both Judaism and Christianity so I think that would give you a wonderful background to everything
that you're reading in your study Bibles and hopefully that is uh enough to keep you busy for years to come
